summary.summary: St Helens ran a deliberately under-borrowed book in 2025/26, funding capital spend from its own cash while taking one £25m PWLB loan in April 2025 at 4.59% to lock in a rate — and the report warns more borrowing 'will be required imminently' for capital schemes. Debt stood at £157.5m at 31 March 2026 against a £220.7m borrowing need, with investments of £97.2m (including £15.1m held for Merseyside Recycling and Waste Authority and £10.3m for schools). Net treasury costs came in £2.8m under budget at £1.8m, helped by deferred borrowing and above-benchmark investment returns. £15m of LOBO loans are profiled at their next lender call dates, which makes the maturity ladder look short-term even though contractual maturities exceed 50 years.

signals.headline: £15m of LOBO loans profiled at their next lender call dates (treated as near-term maturities at 31 March 2026; contractual maturities are over 50 years)
signals.why: At each call date the lender can propose a higher rate, forcing the council to accept it or repay £15m at short notice.

signals.headline: £25m new PWLB loan taken April 2025 at 4.59%, with further borrowing flagged as required 'imminently' for capital schemes funded through borrowing
signals.why: A long-deferred external borrowing programme is now starting, converting internal borrowing into real market demand.

news_drafts.headline: St Helens schools deficit forecast at £20.897m by March 2027 after £11.258m High Needs Stability Grant approved
news_drafts.lead:
St Helens Council forecasts a deficit of £20.897m on its dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, at 31 March 2027. The Department for Education approved an £11.258m High Needs Stability Grant for the council on 2 October 2026.

The department approved the council's Local SEND Reform Plan, enabling access to a grant equal to 90% of the accumulated deficit. SEND stands for special educational needs and disabilities. The grant will reduce the deficit of £12.509m that existed at 31 March 2026, leaving a net prior-year deficit of £1.251m. The in-year pressure on the grant is forecast at £19.646m. Within that, the council forecasts a High Needs overspend of £20.024m. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps a schools-funding deficit off the main balance sheet, remains in place until 31 March 2028. The paper states that the department's assessment found further work is needed on governance, delivery capacity, performance management and partnership arrangements.

Separately, the capital programme budget for the Broad Oak SEND provision scheme is reduced from £1.597m to £155k, a reprofiling of £1.442m. The paper says "Requirements relating to the delivery of this scheme are currently being reviewed" to ensure the optimal solutions are identified.

news_drafts.headline: St. Helens reports £12.509m schools deficit at March 2026; government grant to cover 90% of it
news_drafts.lead:
St. Helens Council had a deficit of £12.509m on its dedicated schools grant at 31 March 2026, according to a report to its Audit and Governance Committee on 23 November. The grant is the government money that funds schools, and the paper says the deficit arises from pressures on high needs, the part that funds special educational needs. The deficit is held in a separate reserve under the statutory override, the temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off the main balance sheet, which continues until March 2028.

The government has announced a High Needs Stability grant that will fund 90% of the deficit at 31 March 2026. The paper says this is subject to approval by the Department for Education of a Local SEND Reform plan.

The committee is also asked to approve the council's updated Annual Governance Statement for 2025/26, the council's own account of how it is run. At the request of its external auditor, Grant Thornton, further details in red text have been added to pages 10 and 11 about the published SEND Inspection Priority Action Plan, which Cabinet approved on 2 September 2026. The paper does not state the outcome of the inspection.

news_drafts.headline: St Helens secures £11.258m high needs grant; schools deficit forecast at £20.897m by March 2027
news_drafts.lead:
The Department for Education approved St Helens Council's Local special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) Reform Plan on 2 October 2026, allowing the council to access an £11.258m High Needs Stability Grant. The grant is equal to 90% of the council's accumulated deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, at 31 March 2026. It is due to be paid at the end of November 2026.

A paper to cabinet puts that deficit at £12.509m at 31 March 2026 and forecasts it at £20.897m at 31 March 2027, after the grant. The paper forecasts an in-year pressure on the grant of £19.646m, with the high needs block, the part that funds SEND, forecast to overspend by £20.024m. It says the deficit is held in a separate reserve and does not affect the General Fund. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off the main balance sheet, remains in place until 31 March 2028. The paper adds that the Department's assessment concluded further work is required on governance, delivery capacity, performance management and partnership arrangements.

The Children & Young People portfolio forecasts a £12.269m overspend for 2026/27, up from £7.617m at Period 1. The paper cites rising costs for looked after children and care leavers, particularly external residential, fostering and supported accommodation placements, and rising SEND demand, including home to school transport and specialist provision. Separately, the 2026/27 capital budget for Broad Oak SEND provision falls from £1.597m to £155k, with £1.442m reprofiled out of the year while the requirements for delivering the scheme are reviewed.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 pay award settled at 3.3% against a 3.0% budget provision, with the 0.3% gap to be met from the vacancy factor.
findings.detail: The paper says the 0.3% difference will be covered by increasing the in-year vacancy factor across services and reports no specific pay award variance. Its recruitment controls and agency staffing approvals are described as part of in-year financial controls.
findings.matters: A pay award above the budgeted rate, absorbed through vacancy savings, shows how a council is funding unbudgeted pay costs within existing budgets.
findings.quote: The resulting 0.3% funding gap will be mitigated through an increase in the existing in-year vacancy factor across services

findings.headline: The Council states it has a potential of up to £1.1m per year in additional health funding for children's placements, subject to Continuing Healthcare eligibility.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council is working with the Integrated Care Board to review high-cost placements and support packages against Continuing Healthcare criteria. It describes this as a potential mitigation that remains subject to assessment and agreement with health partners.
findings.matters: A possible recurring health contribution to high-cost children's placements would offset part of the overspend if confirmed.
findings.figures: Potential additional health funding up to £1.1m per annum; Children & Young People forecast pressure £12.269m
findings.quote: Initial assessments suggest there may be potential for additional health funding of up to £1.1m per annum should eligibility be confirmed.

findings.headline: The Council has been told of an additional audit fee for the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, which has yet to be confirmed.
findings.detail: The external auditors have said the additional fee relates to extra work arising from a member of the public raising questions about the accounts during the public inspection period. The amount has not yet been confirmed.
findings.matters: Public questions about accounts that lead to additional audit work and fees are a relevant signal for other councils and for those relying on the accounts.
findings.figures: Additional fee amount not yet confirmed
findings.quote: The Council's external auditors have informed the Council there will be an additional fee for the audit of the Statement of Accounts 2025/26.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care & Health forecasts a £1.500m overspend, with the number of care reviews down 35% since 2025-2026.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the pressure mainly to cost rather than volume: average package costs rose 4% and complex residential and nursing packages rose 16%. It says sickness and absence have cut review volumes, and the paper estimates the net budget impact at about £1m if this continues.
findings.matters: A fall in care reviews reduces the savings route the department relies on, so the cost pressure may persist through the year.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care overspend £1.500m; review volume down 35%; average package cost up 4%; complex residential and nursing cost up 16%; estimated budget impact c.£1m; demand management savings £2.76m
findings.quote: However, significant levels of sickness and absence within the department has resulted in the volume of reviews being undertaken having fallen by 35% since 2025-2026.

findings.headline: School capital schemes have £4.653m reprofiled from 2026/27 into future years.
findings.detail: The paper says most of the slippage relates to uncommitted grant allocations, with several condition schemes now expected to start or complete in 2027/28. Some project requirements are also under review before delivery proceeds.
findings.matters: Slippage of uncommitted grant spend shows where a capital programme is not delivering in the planned year, which other finance officers will recognise.
findings.figures: Reprofiled from 2026/27 £4.653m; Children & Young People capital 2026/27 £7.134m; 2027/28 £20.216m
findings.quote: The schools capital programme at Period 2 includes a reprofiling of £4.653m from 2026/27 into future years.
